name: Annibale de Gasparis
teaser: The Italian astronomer who discovered nine asteroids, including Hygiea and Parthenope, and made painstaking observations of Mars that helped locate the Red Planet's canals. He later directed the Naples observatory and served in parliament.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how de Gasparis discovered nine main-belt asteroids from Naples in the mid-1800s. Write what asteroids are, where the main belt lies, and why 19th-century astronomers hunted them.

name: John Couch Adams
teaser: The English mathematician who predicted the position of Neptune by calculation alone — though credit went to the Frenchman Le Verrier, who published first. A quiet genius whose math found a planet in the sky.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Adams and Le Verrier independently used Uranus's wobbles to predict Neptune's location. Write how the discovery was confirmed by telescope in 1846 and how the two men shared the credit.

name: Karl Schwarzschild
teaser: The German physicist who solved Einstein's field equations for a point mass while serving on the Russian front in 1916 — finding the exact solution for what we now call a black hole. He died months later, aged 42.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Schwarzschild derived the first exact solution to Einstein's equations and its event horizon. Write what the Schwarzschild radius is and how his wartime paper predicted black holes.

name: Hans Geiger
teaser: The German physicist who built the counter that clicks when radiation passes — the Geiger counter — and who, with Marsden, ran the gold foil experiments that revealed the atomic nucleus. A practical man who made the invisible audible.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Geiger and Müller's counter tube amplifies the tiny ionization from each radioactive particle into a click. Write how the Geiger–Marsden experiment revealed the nucleus and how counters are used today.

name: Johannes van der Waals
teaser: The Dutch physicist who corrected the ideal gas law for real molecules with size and attraction — the van der Waals forces that make geckos stick and liquids condense. He won the 1910 Nobel for his equation of state.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how van der Waals accounted for molecular size and attraction in his gas equation. Write what van der Waals forces are, with a real example like gecko feet or water droplets, and why they matter.

name: Joseph Fourier
teaser: The French mathematician who showed that any signal, no matter how jagged, can be built from smooth sine waves — the Fourier transform that powers audio, images, and every smartphone. He also invented the greenhouse effect concept in his heat studies.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how the Fourier transform decomposes any waveform into its frequencies. Write how it underlies JPEG images, MP3 audio, and WiFi, and how Fourier connected heat flow to Earth's temperature.

name: George Green
teaser: The English miller who taught himself mathematics and, in 1828, published the theorems that today underpin electromagnetism, fluid flow, and computer graphics — while running his family's windmill. He was so obscure his paper was ignored for decades.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn Green's theorem, relating the circulation around a curve to the sum inside it. Write where Green's functions are used today, from physics to machine learning, and why his miller's life delayed his fame.

name: William Bateson
teaser: The English geneticist who coined the word 'genetics' and championed Mendel's laws in England against fierce resistance. He also discovered genetic linkage — the fact that some traits travel together — the first crack in Mendelian independence.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Bateson translated and defended Mendel's work and coined 'genetics' in 1905. Write what linkage is and why his discovery complicated the simple rules of inheritance.

name: Hugo de Vries
teaser: The Dutch botanist who rediscovered Mendel's laws independently and proposed the mutation theory of evolution — sudden jumps in species. He introduced the word 'mutation' and worked with the evening primrose that showed heritable leaps.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how de Vries observed sudden new forms in evening primroses and coined 'mutation.' Write how his idea complemented natural selection and how modern genetics reframed his findings.

name: Wilhelm Johannsen
teaser: The Danish botanist who coined the terms 'gene,' 'genotype,' and 'phenotype' — separating what an organism inherits from what it shows. His bean experiments showed selection acts only on the genotype's variation.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Johannsen's self-fertilized bean lines proved that selection cannot change a pure genotype. Write the difference between genotype and phenotype and why his naming of the 'gene' mattered.

name: Hermann Muller
teaser: The American geneticist who proved X-rays cause mutations, founding radiation genetics and earning the 1946 Nobel. A tireless campaigner, he warned early about the genetic dangers of radiation — and later of nuclear fallout.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Muller exposed fruit flies to X-rays and measured a leap in mutation rates. Write why his 1927 result was shocking and how it shaped radiation safety standards.

name: Alfred Hershey
teaser: The American phage geneticist who, with Martha Chase, used radioactive labels to prove that DNA — not protein — carries genetic information. The 'blender experiment' of 1952 settled the identity of the hereditary material.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Hershey and Chase labeled phage DNA and protein with different isotopes and blended the shells off bacteria. Write how the radioactivity that entered cells identified DNA as the genetic material.

name: Oswald Avery
teaser: The Canadian-American physician who, with MacLeod and McCarty, showed in 1944 that DNA transforms bacteria — the first solid evidence that genes are made of DNA. His cautious paper was largely ignored until the double helix.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Avery's team purified the transforming substance from bacteria and identified it as DNA. Write what the transformation experiment showed and why scientists were slow to accept it.

name: George Beadle
teaser: The American geneticist who, with Tatum, showed that each gene controls one enzyme — the one gene–one enzyme hypothesis — by mutating bread mold with X-rays. He shared the 1958 Nobel for linking genes to chemistry.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Beadle and Tatum's Neurospora experiments linked single genes to single enzymes. Write how they used X-ray mutants and growth media and why the one gene–one enzyme idea launched biochemical genetics.

name: Edward Tatum
teaser: The American biochemist who joined Beadle in the bread mold experiments and later discovered that bacteria exchange genes — bacterial conjugation — opening the door to bacterial genetics and recombinant DNA.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Tatum and Lederberg found that E. coli strains can exchange genetic material. Write what bacterial conjugation is and how it enabled the later recombinant DNA revolution.

name: Joshua Lederberg
teaser: The American geneticist who showed bacteria can have sex — conjugation — at age 23, and went on to explore space biology and artificial intelligence in medicine. He shared the 1958 Nobel and warned of emerging infections.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Lederberg and Tatum proved bacteria exchange genes by physical contact. Write what conjugation is, how it spreads antibiotic resistance, and how Lederberg pioneered biosecurity thinking.

name: Frederick Griffith
teaser: The British bacteriologist who, in 1928, discovered bacterial transformation: dead virulent pneumococci could pass their deadly trait to live harmless ones. His mystery — the 'transforming principle' — was later solved as DNA.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Griffith's mouse experiments showed a heat-killed strain could transform a live one. Write what his 1928 finding implied and how Avery, then Hershey and Chase, identified the transforming substance.

name: Nettie Stevens
teaser: The American geneticist who discovered that sex is determined by chromosomes — XX for female, XY for male — in 1905, by studying mealworm cells. Long overlooked, she quietly answered a question that had stumped biology.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Stevens found that female and male mealworms differ by one chromosome pair. Write how the XX/XY system works in humans and why her discovery took decades to be credited.

name: E. B. Wilson
teaser: The American cytologist whose book The Cell in Development and Heredity organized all of cell biology, and whose studies of sex chromosomes helped confirm the chromosomal theory of inheritance alongside Stevens and Morgan.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how E. B. Wilson synthesized cell division, fertilization, and heredity in his landmark book. Write what the chromosomal theory of inheritance states and how Wilson's teaching shaped American biology.

name: Harold Urey
teaser: The American chemist who discovered deuterium, heavy hydrogen, and won the 1934 Nobel — then turned to the origin of life, showing with Stanley Miller how lightning in a primitive atmosphere could make amino acids.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Urey found deuterium in distilled water and later designed the Miller–Urey experiment on life's origins. Write what the experiment produced and what it suggests about how life began.

name: Stanley Miller
teaser: The American chemist who, as a 23-year-old graduate student, zapped a flask of methane, ammonia, and water with sparks and produced amino acids — the building blocks of life — in a week. The Miller–Urey experiment electrified the world.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Miller's spark-discharge apparatus simulated lightning on the early Earth. Write what amino acids appeared, what the experiment proved about abiogenesis, and how later reanalyses refined its conclusions.

name: George Wald
teaser: The American biochemist who worked out the chemistry of vision — how vitamin A and retinal absorb light in the retina — and shared the 1967 Nobel. He later became a leading voice against nuclear weapons.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Wald traced the visual cycle in which retinal changes shape when light hits it. Write how rods detect dim light, how color vision works in cones, and why vitamin A is essential for sight.

name: Ralph Steinman
teaser: The Canadian immunologist who discovered dendritic cells — the sentinels that show the immune system what to attack — and won the 2011 Nobel three days after his death. His work underlies modern cancer immunotherapy.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Steinman found the cells that present antigens and awaken T cells. Write how dendritic cells patrol the body and how their discovery led to therapeutic cancer vaccines and checkpoint therapy.

name: Michael Rosbash
teaser: The American geneticist who, with Hall and Young, discovered the molecular clock inside every cell — the genes that keep our daily rhythms in sync with the sun. They shared the 2017 Nobel for unlocking the circadian machinery.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Rosbash's team showed that the period gene and its protein form a feedback loop that ticks every 24 hours. Write how the circadian clock affects sleep, health, and shift work.

name: Jeffrey Hall
teaser: The American geneticist who, with Rosbash and Young, identified the genes behind the body's internal clock and shared the 2017 Nobel. He then left academia and bred show dogs — proving curiosity doesn't retire.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Hall and Rosbash used fruit flies to find the period gene and its feedback loop. Write what happens when clock genes are disrupted and why the Nobel committee honored a fly's sleep.
